newsitem.title: INDIA: Flaming suicide threat haunts Miss World final.
newsitem.headline: Flaming suicide threat haunts Miss World final.

text.p: An Indian woman reissued a threat to upstage Miss World's crowning moment by carrying out a human torch suicide protest after a court said on Tuesday the beauty pageant can go ahead.
One man burnt himself to death last week to protest the show which opponents say offends women and Indian culture.

"My protests will be peaceful. By burning myself I will not be disrupting the show. We will go ahead with our earlier plan," Kina Narayana Shashikala, leader of the Mahila Jagran Samiti (Forum for Awakening Women), told Reuters after a court rejected the group's petition to block the pageant.
The traditionalist group had held its threat of self-immolation in abeyance until the court decision was known.

"We declined to ban the show," R.P. Sethi, chief justice of the Karnataka High Court, told a packed courtroom in the southern city of Bangalore. "The state government should not prevent peaceful protests."

Shashikala has said several of her followers will join the 20,000 people expected to attend the Miss World crowning ceremony on November 23 and take cyanide pills before setting their silk saris ablaze.
"Obviously it is a very sad situation when somebody is prepared to do this without finding out what we are all about," Julia Morley, president of Miss World International, told Reuters.
While the furore surrounding the show continued to build on Tuesday, the 88 contestants were competing for Miss Personality in another sub-event outside Bangalore.
Police plan to deploy 12,000 officers on the final night, and after the court ruling Bangalore Police Commissioner S.C. Burman said they will be reinforced by paramilitary officers.
As if the threat of multiple suicides were not enough, Burman said he had received reports the pageant could also be attacked by splinter cells of the Peoples War Group.
The Maoist rebel group has killed 15 policemen in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh state in recent days.
"We have already deployed the Rapid Action Force and put the National Security Guard on standby," the police chief said.
People attending events at the Miss World gala have been frisked by police, who confiscated cigarette lighters and bags.
In addition to a de facto ban on smoking, the court on Tuesday told pageant organisers that no alcohol should be served at the Chinnaswamy cricket stadium where the open air show is being held.
The finale is expected to be seen by an estimated two billion television viewers worldwide.

A protester against the Michael Jackson concert in Bombay in late October also threatened to burn himself but was detained by police before he could commit suicide. Under Indian law, police can take people into custody as a preventive measure.
A police chief and senior court official were assigned by the high court to watch the beauty parade on Saturday to ensure there is no indecent exposure of bodies, nudity or obscenity.
"Absolutely. I agree with that wholeheartedly," Julia Morley said when informed of the ruling.

The ruling Janata Dal in Karnataka, which is Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's party, has supported Miss World coming to their state capital, which is known as India's "Garden City", but any politicians hoping for a free ticket can think again.
The court said anyone in the state government will have to pay like anyone else.

Tickets for the three-hour show, which will involve nearly 500 dancers, performers, and elephants on an elaborate giant set based on Indian temples, cost between 1,900 and 25,000 rupees ($53 to $700). ($1.00=35.75 rupees)
